title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Folate synthesis. Sulfonamides and trimethoprim block two successive steps of folic acid synthesis, a synergistic combination (co-trimoxazole).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell membrane. Polymyxins (colistin) disrupt the Gram-negative membranes; daptomycin acts on Gram-positive membranes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nucleic acid synthesis. Quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV; rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase; metronidazole damages DNA in anaerobes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 30S ribosomal subunit. Aminoglycosides (bactericidal, cause misreading) and tetracyclines (bacteriostatic) bind the small subunit.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 50S ribosomal subunit. Macrolides, lincosamides, streptogramins and chloramphenicol bind the large subunit; mostly bacteriostatic.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Cell wall synthesis. β-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, glycopeptides bind the peptidoglycan precursor and fosfomycin blocks an early step; all are bactericidal.
Antibiotic: selective, systemic, slow, low mg/L. Antiseptic: non-selective, local, fast, high %.
G/V (natural), M (anti-staphylococcal: oxacillin, cloxacillin), A (ampicillin, amoxicillin), carboxy/ureido (piperacillin, anti-Pseudomonas).
1st Gram+; 2nd more Gram-; 3rd strong Gram- (ceftriaxone), not enterococci/Listeria; 4th cefepime; 5th ceftaroline (MRSA).
Carbapenems: widest spectrum, ESBL-stable, reserve. Aztreonam: aerobic Gram-negatives only.
30S: aminoglycosides, tetracyclines. 50S: macrolides, lincosamides, streptogramins, chloramphenicol.
Quinolones (gyrase, topo IV), rifampicin (RNA polymerase), metronidazole (anaerobe DNA), sulfonamide + trimethoprim (folate).
Mixed infections, broader cover, synergy, preventing resistance.
Enzymatic inactivation, target modification, reduced permeability, efflux.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Catarrhal stage. One to two weeks of coryza, low fever and a mild worsening cough; bacteria are most abundant and transmission is highest.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Convalescent stage. Gradual recovery over weeks to months as the cough becomes less frequent and milder.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis by stage. PCR on a posterior nasopharyngeal swab is first line, most sensitive early; culture is the gold standard but slow and insensitive; serology is only retrospective.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Paroxysmal stage. Two to six weeks or more of rapid repeated coughs ending in an inspiratory whoop, post-tussive vomiting, exhaustion and, in infants, apnoea; worse at night.
Strictly human, contagious, droplet spread, small Gram-negative coccobacillus, strict aerobe, fastidious, asaccharolytic.
Filamentous haemagglutinin, fimbriae (FIM2/3), pertactin, tracheal colonisation factor.
Pertussis toxin (lymphocytosis, immune effects), tracheal cytotoxin (ciliostasis), adenylate cyclase toxin (phagocytes), dermonecrotic toxin, LPS.
Catarrhal 1-2 wk (most contagious); paroxysmal 2-6 wk (whoop, vomiting, apnoea); convalescent weeks-months.
Posterior nasopharyngeal Dacron/flocked swab or aspirate, straight into Amies-charcoal or Regan-Lowe transport.
Regan-Lowe or Bordet-Gengou, 35-37 °C, humid, no CO₂, 7-10 days; mercury-drop colonies.
Macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin, clarithromycin); TMP-SMX alternative; early treatment cuts transmission.
Whole-cell DTP (pentavalent) at 2, 3, 4 months; boosters at 18 months and 5 years.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aberrant bodies. Under stress such as interferon-γ, enlarged non-dividing forms persist, linked to chronic inflammation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Maturation and release. Reticulate bodies turn back into elementary bodies, which are released to infect new epithelial cells or macrophages.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Elementary body. The small, metabolically inactive, infectious form that survives outside cells and attaches to host cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inclusion. After endocytosis-like uptake, the EB stays inside a vacuole whose fusion with lysosomes it blocks, using inclusion membrane (Inc) proteins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reticulate body. The larger, metabolically active, non-infectious form that multiplies by binary fission, drawing ATP from the host cell.
Obligate intracellular, strictly human, droplet spread, no classical peptidoglycan, energy parasite.
EB: small, infectious, inert, extracellular survival. RB: larger, replicative, non-infectious, intracellular.
MOMP/OMPs (entry), Inc proteins (inclusion), type III secretion, phagolysosome fusion block, LPS, proteases.
Mostly asymptomatic; pharyngitis, sinusitis, bronchitis, atypical pneumonia; asthma, COPD, atherosclerosis links.
PCR (ompA, 16S rRNA, incA) of nasopharyngeal samples; MIF serology (slow); DFA rarely.
IgM about 3 weeks after onset; IgG diagnostic at 6-8 weeks.
Macrolides; doxycycline or fluoroquinolone alternatives; >10-14 days; β-lactams ineffective.
No vaccine; respiratory and hand hygiene, avoiding contact, ventilation, early treatment.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli. Produces Shiga toxins (Stx1, Stx2): abundant bloody diarrhoea without leucocytes; toxins can spread systemically and cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Enteroinvasive E. coli. Closely related to Shigella: invades colonic cells via M cells with invasion plasmid antigens, spreads cell to cell, causing dysentery with fever and leucocytes in stools.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Enteropathogenic E. coli. Attaches to enterocytes and effaces microvilli without systemic spread; specific serotypes cause infantile gastroenteritis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Enterotoxigenic E. coli. Heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) enterotoxins make the gut secrete fluid; purely toxin-mediated, non-inflammatory watery diarrhoea (traveller's diarrhoea).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extra-intestinal E. coli. Uropathogenic strains with pili cause about 90% of urinary infections; K1-capsulated strains cause most neonatal meningitis and many neonatal septicaemias.
Gram-negative bacilli, oxidase −, nitrate +, glucose fermenters, facultative anaerobes, non-sporing.
Obligate: Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, some E. coli. Opportunistic: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Serratia, Proteus.
UTI (~90%), neonatal meningitis/sepsis (K1), intra-abdominal, bone, skin, septicaemia.
ETEC (LT/ST toxins), EPEC (infants), EIEC (invasive dysentery), EHEC (Shiga toxin, HUS), EAEC, DAEC.
Guided by antibiogram; high ESBL rates; fosfomycin/nitrofurantoin for cystitis; carbapenems for severe ESBL.
Capsulated, non-motile, mucoid colonies; pneumonia, UTI, septicaemia, nosocomial.
Capsule (>70 types), LPS, fimbriae, siderophores, biofilm, β-lactamases.
Susceptible: pip-tazo/amikacin; ESBL: carbapenem ± amikacin; CRKP: colistin, tigecycline, combinations.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Non-typhoidal Salmonella. Other S. enterica serovars are zoonotic, reaching humans through poultry, eggs, meat, dairy or contact with animals such as reptiles.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gastroenteritis. Diarrhoea, cramps, vomiting and fever after 6-72 h, usually self-limited; bacteraemia and focal infections mainly in the immunocompromised.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Typhoidal Salmonella. S. Typhi and Paratyphi have humans as their only reservoir and spread through food or water contaminated by patients or carriers.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Enteric fever. Bacteria cross the gut, survive in macrophages and spread to liver, spleen and marrow: sustained high fever, early positive blood cultures, risk of bleeding and perforation; chronic gallbladder carriage.
Motile, lactose −, H₂S +, glucose +, oxidase −, urease −; black-centred colonies on Hektoen/XLD/SS.
Typhoidal: humans only, systemic enteric fever, carriers. Non-typhoidal: zoonotic, gastroenteritis, self-limited.
Acid/bile resistance, T3SS invasion, macrophage survival, bacteraemia, liver/spleen/marrow, gallbladder carriage.
Blood culture in week 1 (80-90%), then stool, urine, bile; agglutination; Widal/ELISA limited.
Ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone or azithromycin; Ty21a oral (4 doses, ≥6 y), Vi injectable (1 dose, ≥2 y).
Enterobacter cloacae, Klebsiella aerogenes: resist ampicillin, co-amoxiclav, C1G, C2G; carbapenems for severe.
Swarming motility, urease +, lactose −; P. mirabilis indole −, P. vulgaris indole +.
Urease → ammonia → alkaline urine → struvite precipitation, catheter encrustation, biofilm.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Conjugation. Direct transfer, usually of a plasmid, from a donor (F+ or Hfr) to a recipient (F-) through a sex pilus; the commonest route in nature.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mobile resistance genes. Genes on plasmids, transposons and integron cassettes can move between bacteria of the same or different species, spreading antibiotic resistance and toxins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transduction. A bacteriophage packages a piece of bacterial DNA and delivers it to the next bacterium it infects.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transformation. A competent bacterium takes up free DNA from its surroundings; shown by Griffith with S. pneumoniae; natural in pneumococcus, Neisseria and Haemophilus.
Chromosome: large circular dsDNA, essential genes. Plasmid: small, autonomous replication, non-essential, special traits.
Conjugative: tra genes, self-transfer (F plasmid). Non-conjugative: mobilised with a conjugative plasmid.
Transposon: jumping gene with its own transposase. Integron: captures cassettes with an integrase; cassettes lack their own enzyme.
Phenotypic: expression change, reversible, not inherited. Genotypic: mutation or transfer, inherited.
Stability, rarity (~10⁻⁹), specificity (one trait), spontaneity.
No, they select pre-existing resistant mutants that then multiply.
Transformation (naked DNA), transduction (phage), conjugation (pilus, plasmid).
F+: F plasmid present. F−: absent. Hfr: F integrated into the chromosome.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plain blood agar. Intact red cells keep V factor locked in and NADases destroy free NAD, so H. influenzae fails to grow; MacConkey lacks both factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chocolate agar. Blood agar heated to lyse red cells, releasing X and V factors and inactivating the NADases: the standard medium for Haemophilus, incubated in 5-10% CO₂.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Satellitism. On blood agar, tiny H. influenzae colonies grow only near a streak of haemolytic S. aureus, which releases V factor (NAD) and haemin from lysed cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: V factor. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD), inside red cells and destroyed by NADases in plain blood agar.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: X factor. Haemin (haematin) from red cells; needed by H. influenzae for its respiratory enzymes.

title: Morphology and habitat of H. influenzae?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: Morphology and habitat of H. influenzae?
body.back: Small pleomorphic Gram-negative coccobacilli; obligate human respiratory parasite; droplet spread.
X = haemin (heat-stable); V = NAD (heat-labile); both needed; chocolate agar supplies them.
Tiny colonies grow near haemolytic S. aureus on blood agar because it releases V factor.
PRP capsule (antiphagocytic), pili, IgA protease, outer membrane proteins, LOS.
Hib: invasive (meningitis, epiglottitis, sepsis, arthritis). Non-typeable: otitis, sinusitis, bronchitis, COPD, conjunctivitis.
Never refrigerate; room temperature; transport medium; within 3 hours.
Invasive: ceftriaxone/cefotaxime. β-lactamase-positive otitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. Contacts: rifampicin.
PRP conjugated to a protein carrier; 2, 4 (6) months + booster at 11-15 months; ~95% drop in meningitis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adhesins. Surface structures that attach bacteria to host cells, such as type 1 pili of E. coli on bladder epithelium or protein F of streptococci binding fibronectin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extracellular enzymes. Hyaluronidase and collagenase open tissues for spread; coagulase forms fibrin shields; kinases dissolve clots.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Survival factors. Siderophores steal iron from lactoferrin and transferrin; IgA proteases (Neisseria, Haemophilus) cleave mucosal IgA; some bacteria block phagosome acidification (mycobacteria, Legionella).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Anti-phagocytic factors. Capsules mask surface targets (pneumococcus, Hib); staphylococcal protein A blocks antibody Fc; leucocidins and streptolysins kill phagocytes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Toxins. Exotoxins: highly toxic, specific proteins that can be turned into toxoids for vaccines. Endotoxin: lipid A of Gram-negative LPS, triggering cytokines, fever and septic shock via CD14/TLR4.
Saprophytism (dead matter), mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (bacterium benefits, host unaffected), parasitism (host harmed).
Resident: deep, persistent, re-establishes, not washable. Transient: superficial, temporary, washable, spreads infection.
Pathogenicity: ability to cause disease. Virulence: its degree, e.g. infectious dose.
Anti-phagocytic factors, adhesins, intracellular survival (iron, IgA protease), toxins, extracellular enzymes.
Exotoxin: secreted protein, very toxic, specific, toxoid possible. Endotoxin: LPS lipid A, Gram-negative, septic shock.
LPS + LBP → CD14/TLR4/MD2 → TNF and cytokines, complement and coagulation activation (DIC) → septic shock.
Toxoids (diphtheria, tetanus), killed (pertussis), live attenuated (BCG), purified antigens (meningococcus, pneumococcus).
Nosocomial: after 48 h in hospital, 5-10% of inpatients, invasive devices. Community: before 48 h, no healthcare link.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clearance. Alveolar macrophages and innate immunity eliminate the bacilli in some exposed people.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Airborne infection. Droplet nuclei from a person with open pulmonary TB carry bacilli deep into the alveoli; M. tuberculosis is a strictly human pathogen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Latent infection. Macrophages and T cells wall off the bacilli in a granuloma; the person is well and not infectious but may have a positive tuberculin or IGRA test.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary active tuberculosis. Progressive disease soon after infection when immunity is weak: young children, HIV, malnutrition.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Reactivation. Latent bacilli reawaken when immunity falls (HIV, malnutrition, age, drugs), causing pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease.
Lipid-rich (mycolic acid) wall retains carbol fuchsin despite acid-alcohol; Ziehl-Neelsen shows red bacilli.
Strictly human, airborne, strict aerobe, catalase +, very slow growth on Löwenstein-Jensen (2-6 weeks).
Clearance, latent infection (granuloma), primary active TB, reactivation later.
Early-morning fasting sputum ×3, bronchial or gastric aspirates.
Direct: microscopy, culture, NAAT (GeneXpert), antigen. Indirect: tuberculin skin test, IGRA.
Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (+ streptomycin).
2RHZE / 4RH: 2 months of four drugs, 4 months of rifampicin + isoniazid; DOT.
Case finding and treatment, contact screening, BCG at birth.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Natural resistance. Drugs acting on peptidoglycan (β-lactams, glycopeptides, fosfomycin) have no target.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Culture. Needs rich media with sterols (SP-4, PPLO, modified Hayflick), CO₂ and 6-20 days for M. pneumoniae; rarely done clinically; tiny 'fried-egg' colonies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram stain. Without a wall they do not stain usefully by Gram and take variable coccoid or filamentous shapes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Wall-less bacteria. Class Mollicutes ('soft skin'): no peptidoglycan wall, a cholesterol-containing membrane, 0.3-0.85 µm, the smallest organisms able to multiply on their own.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Diagnosis and treatment. PCR on throat or nasopharyngeal samples is the method of choice; treatment uses macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones.
No cell wall, sterol membrane, smallest self-replicating prokaryotes, pleomorphic, not Gram-stainable.
M. pneumoniae: respiratory, atypical pneumonia. M. hominis: PID, pyelonephritis, postpartum fever. Ureaplasma: NGU, PID.
Cytadherence organelle, variable surface proteins, CARDS toxin, H₂O₂, biofilm.
Rich sterol media (SP-4, PPLO, Hayflick), CO₂, 37 °C; 6-20 days; rarely done.
PCR on throat/nasopharyngeal samples (gold standard); serology on paired sera.
β-lactams and all drugs acting on peptidoglycan synthesis.
Macrolides, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones (macrolides in children).
IgM autoantibodies against red cells that agglutinate at low temperature; associated with M. pneumoniae.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Invasive disease. Entry into the blood gives bacteraemia and sepsis, most dangerous in infants, the elderly and people without a spleen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Local spread. Extension to the middle ear, sinuses (common in young children) and lungs: pneumococcus is the commonest cause of community pneumonia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Meningitis. Bacteria reaching the CSF cause purulent meningitis, treated with high-dose ceftriaxone plus vancomycin until susceptibility is known.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Nasopharyngeal carriage. Pneumococci colonise the upper airway without symptoms, spread by droplets; viral infection or immune weakness allows disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Virulence factors. The polysaccharide capsule blocks C3b binding (antiphagocytic, >90 serotypes); pneumolysin lyses cells; autolysin releases it; IgA protease, neuraminidase and surface proteins aid colonisation.
Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci; commensal of the nasopharynx; droplet spread.
α-haemolytic, catalase −, optochin sensitive, bile soluble; mucoid draughtsman colonies in CO₂.
Capsule (blocks C3b), pneumolysin, autolysin, PspA/PspC, neuraminidase, hyaluronidase, IgA1 protease.
The wall C polysaccharide precipitates with C-reactive protein, a marker of inflammation.
Pneumonia, otitis media, sinusitis, bacteraemia/sepsis, meningitis.
Immunochromatographic C-polysaccharide antigen test; PCR for lytA, ply, cps.
Mild: amoxicillin. Severe: IV penicillin/ampicillin or ceftriaxone. Meningitis: ceftriaxone + vancomycin.
Polysaccharide linked to protein becomes T-dependent, so infants respond; 3 doses from 2 months in Morocco.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Pneumococcus. α-haemolytic (green), optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble: Streptococcus pneumoniae.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Group A streptococcus. β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive, PYR-positive, Lancefield group A: Streptococcus pyogenes.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Catalase-positive cocci. Staphylococci, in clusters; coagulase then separates S. aureus from coagulase-negative species.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Group B streptococcus. β-haemolytic, bacitracin-resistant, CAMP-positive and hippurate-positive: Streptococcus agalactiae.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram-positive cocci. Starting point: purple cocci on Gram stain; the catalase test splits staphylococci from streptococci.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Catalase-negative cocci. Streptococci and enterococci, in chains or pairs; blood agar haemolysis is the next step.
A: S. pyogenes. B: S. agalactiae (neonates). D: enterococci, S. bovis. F/G/L: S. anginosus (abscesses).
β: complete clear zone (S. pyogenes). α: green partial (pneumococcus). γ: none (enterococcus).
Catalase −, β-haemolytic, bacitracin S, PYR +, group A, CAMP −, hippurate −.
M protein, hyaluronic capsule, protein F, streptolysins O/S, streptokinase, DNase, superantigens (Spe).
Pharyngitis, scarlet fever, impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotising fasciitis, STSS, puerperal sepsis.
Rheumatic fever (after pharyngitis, mimicry) and glomerulonephritis (after throat or skin, immune complexes).
Penicillin (no resistance), amoxicillin in children; macrolide or clindamycin if allergic; 10 days for pharyngitis.
IV penicillin + clindamycin, surgical debridement, supportive care.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram-negative wall. Thin peptidoglycan in a periplasmic space, covered by an outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) and porins.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram-negative result. Alcohol disrupts the outer membrane and the thin wall releases the dye; the safranin counterstain makes cells pink.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram-positive wall. Thick peptidoglycan with teichoic and lipoteichoic acids and no outer membrane.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Gram-positive result. The thick peptidoglycan traps the crystal violet-iodine complex during alcohol decolorisation, so cells stay purple.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Peptidoglycan. Alternating N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid chains cross-linked by short peptides; β-lactams block the penicillin-binding proteins that build it, so the cell bursts.
Prokaryote: 0.2-5 µm, nucleoid, no organelles, 70S ribosomes, circular chromosome, peptidoglycan wall, binary fission.
Anti-phagocytic virulence factor, rapid diagnosis (soluble antigens), serotypes, vaccines (Hib, pneumococcus).
Positive: thick PG, teichoic acids. Negative: thin PG, periplasm, outer membrane with LPS and porins.
Fimbriae: adhesion. Pili: longer, conjugation. Flagella: motility, H antigen.
Obligate aerobes, obligate anaerobes, facultative anaerobes, aerotolerant anaerobes, microaerophiles.

title: Types of culture media by use?
subject: subj:bacterio1

body.front: Types of culture media by use?
body.back: Simple, enriched, selective, enrichment, differential, transport.
Lag, exponential (log), stationary, death.
Respiration: inorganic final acceptor (O₂ or nitrate), up to 38 ATP. Fermentation: organic acceptor, 2 ATP.
